note: Generated from git history by build_updates.py. A round is here if and only if it was committed; this log cannot drift from what shipped.

rounds.title: Two panels instead of four, a readable readout, and a flight between the views
rounds.summary: GROUND CHROME. Four floating cards over a rendered world are four things asking to be read before the world is. The rails now hold one panel each: snapshot and tour on the left, cursor readout, layers and legend on the right. The legend folds — it is reference, read once, and then it is in the way. The tour says how many places it has, because the list is taller than its box and without the count it just looks like it ends wherever the window cuts it.

rounds.title: INDEX: the whole atlas as one image, and vitality as a shape
rounds.summary: A third view. The ground says where a language is and the genealogy says what it is related to; neither says how many there are or how unevenly they are held. 7,672 cells, one per language, squarified into their families.

rounds.title: A tree that can be read: no overprinting, a depth axis, ribbons you can see through
rounds.summary: Four defects in the genealogy view, all of them the same kind — a claim drawn without the geometry to support it.

rounds.title: A search that finds languages, and a spine for the long cards
rounds.summary: TWO OF THE SEVEN. Both were gaps a visitor hits in the first minute.

rounds.title: The shape check was measuring the wrong image, and it had been all along
rounds.summary: Удмурт кыл's plate was a photograph of a media-school class with an 1882 Udmurt alphabet sitting unused at slot 1. The subject rule had correctly chosen the alphabet. Something put it back.

rounds.title: An advertisement is not an artefact, even when it advertises books
rounds.summary: August flagged the Goan Konkani plate twice and I noted it twice without removing it. It was a hoarding with a phone number on it — "Books offered for sale by the kilo, in Goa" — and the text on the board is MARATHI, in Kolhapur, which is neither Goa nor Konkani. Wrong on every axis.

rounds.title: A card opens at the top, and Paniya was a spring in Crimea
rounds.summary: TWO THINGS AUGUST FOUND.

rounds.title: A name is not a URI, and "harp" is not "harpiste"
rounds.summary: Two things August spotted.

rounds.title: Family and branch cards get objects: 0 branch cards illustrated to 22, 1,054 objects total
rounds.summary: August asked for images across all families AND branches. The branches had none — 202 authored branch cards and not one object between them, because only families with a hand-written subject were ever queued. Branch nodes are interior nodes and almost none of them appear in the family record the queue was built from, which is why a first attempt at this queued four subjects and illustrated nothing.

rounds.title: Adding images: 952 objects across 327 languages, and the filter that made them usable
rounds.summary: 873 objects / 297 languages -> 952 / 327. Plus 44 hand-authored named artefacts, which are the ones worth naming: the Jelling runestones for Danish, the Seyðabrævið of 1298 for Faroese, the Shinpukuji-bon Kojiki for Japanese and Old Japanese, and for Tagalog the Librong pagaaralan nang manga Tagalog nang uicang Castila.

rounds.title: The plate has a higher bar than the wall, keyboards are gone, and images cache by title
rounds.summary: AUGUST'S IMAGE RULES, ENCODED. The main image for a language should be writing, a book, a cultural artefact or a landmark. A street sign or an advertisement is real evidence of a language in use and belongs in the card — but not as the first thing seen, because it says "somebody printed this here" rather than "this is what the language looks like". So plates are now scored: manuscripts, inscriptions, codices, alphabets, primers and books to the front; signs, adverts, posters and placards to the back. Nothing is discarded. 108 plates reordered.

rounds.title: Genealogy is the front door, the ground card stops following you, and an update log
rounds.summary: THREE THINGS AUGUST ASKED FOR.

rounds.title: The fixable gap is zero: every language with a published grammar now carries something
rounds.summary: 34 labels, and they are the last ones this measurement can ask for. Atlas-wide, no language with a full published grammar carries nothing but a composed description any more. What is still bare — 1,552 of 7,672 — is bare because nobody has written a grammar of it, and the MED breakdown says so exactly: 0 at level 0, 0 at level 1, the rest at level 2 and below.

rounds.title: Five families that had no labels at all now have some
rounds.summary: Nilotic, Cariban, Nakh-Daghestanian, Salishan and Central Sudanic held 222 languages between them and not one authored label. 25 labels across those five plus the largest unlabelled in Mayan, Quechuan and Algic. 632 labels, 434 cited.

rounds.title: Tamil gets a label, seven families get branch cards, and rule 11 gets enforced
rounds.summary: TAMIL had no label. Seventy-five million speakers, two thousand years of continuous literature, and the only language of India whose classical corpus is read without translation by ordinary speakers today — the Sangam poems are secular, love and war rather than scripture, which is unusual for a classical literature anywhere.

rounds.title: The gallery was shipping rejected images under the replacement's caption
rounds.summary: THE DEFECT, and it is the worst class this project has had.

rounds.title: 29 timelines for Atlantic-Congo and Austronesian: 940 events to 1,033
rounds.summary: These two families are 2,684 of the 8,618 languages here and they carried seven dated events.

rounds.title: Austronesian opened: 32 labels and 27 branch cards for the family whose tree is its argument
rounds.summary: 1,276 languages and 25 labels, no branch cards.

rounds.title: Atlantic-Congo opened: 32 labels and 22 branch cards for the largest family here
rounds.summary: 1,408 languages — a fifth of this atlas — and it carried 24 labels and no branch cards at all.

rounds.title: Pama-Nyungan closed: 38 labels, 20 branch cards, 20 timelines, from zero of each
rounds.summary: Three families now have no language with a full published grammar and nothing here: Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan and Pama-Nyungan. Pama-Nyungan started this session with nothing at all.

rounds.title: Pama-Nyungan gets its first labels; Sino-Tibetan closes to zero
rounds.summary: Sino-Tibetan now has no language with a full published grammar and nothing here. That was 15 — mostly languages of a few thousand speakers in Yunnan, Sichuan and the Tibetan marches, several described for the first time in the last decade. Lamo got its first full description in 2019. The Lalo languages were shown to be several languages rather than dialects of one only in 2011, on a survey of sixty villages. Tosu, of all of them, has its own logographic script.

rounds.title: 30 Sino-Tibetan branch cards, 37 timelines, and a branch card that had been counting the layout
rounds.summary: BRANCH CARDS. Sino-Tibetan had none of the 61 — every fork in its tree read "branch of the Sino-Tibetan language family". Thirty now: Sinitic, Lolo-Burmese, Loloish, Burmish, Kuki-Chin, Angami-Ao, Patkaian, Bodish, Kiranti, Karenic, Qiangic, Gyalrongic, Lisoid, Nisoid and the rest.

rounds.title: Indo-European closed; Sino-Tibetan opened with 26 labels
rounds.summary: INDO-EUROPEAN IS DONE, on a stopping condition that can be checked rather than a feeling.

rounds.title: 18 closing labels, and three defects the gallery had been hiding
rounds.summary: THE LABELS. Every Indo-European language with a full published grammar that still carried nothing here but a composed description — eighteen of them. A grammar exists for each, so their emptiness was our gap, not the record's: Hieroglyphic Luwian, Middle Low German (the language of the Hanse, which gave the Scandinavian languages a quarter of their everyday vocabulary), Old Marathi, Macanese, and the Caribbean and Pacific creoles — Trinidadian, Tobagonian, Antiguan, San Andres, Limonese, Tayo. 399 -> 417 labels.

rounds.title: 40 more Indo-European timelines: 103 languages and 544 events to 143 and 710
rounds.summary: Timelines for the languages labelled in pass 4, where the record fixes real dates.

rounds.title: Speaker counts as real triples, and a gate that catches a builder that died
rounds.summary: Rule 14 says every speaker count is (value, year, source). Two of the three were being kept.

rounds.title: Indo-European pass 4: phrases for the ancient languages, a citation on every label
rounds.summary: The three things this pass was for.

rounds.title: Indo-European pass 3: 98% of its languages now have written context, not just a classification
rounds.summary: 403 of Indo-European's 586 languages had nothing but a word list. Authoring 403 labels is not possible; what those languages have in common is that they are clusters — 19 ending in English, 11 in French, the Romani varieties, the Indo-Aryan zones — and a cluster shares a history.

rounds.title: Indo-European pass 2: 39 timelines, 200 more dated events
rounds.summary: 90 Indo-European languages carried a museum label and no dated events at all. 39 now have one — the ones with the most active writing communities — and the timeline tier goes from 64 languages and 344 events to 103 and 544.

rounds.title: Indo-European, pass 1: 61 branch descriptions, 34 new labels with sources, and a test that was too loose
rounds.summary: August: cards were reading "branch of the Indo-European language family" and "A Sino-Tibetan language". He is right that those say nothing — they restate the tree.

rounds.title: Every audit finished: 278 images rejected by eye, and four other tiers checked
rounds.summary: GALLERY, COMPLETE. Seven plate sheets and twelve wall sheets, every object in the collection laid out and looked at. 278 files rejected, 76 (language, subject) pairs retired, all recorded in data/gallery/rejected.json. 1,487 objects when this audit began, 823 now across 269 languages.

rounds.title: The wall objects, first four sheets: 43 more rejected
rounds.summary: The plates were audited; the objects behind them had never been looked at. 575 of them, twelve contact sheets, and audit_gallery.py grew a --walls mode so the plates already cleared are not re-read.

rounds.title: The audit finished: 175 images rejected by eye, and the alphabets audited too
rounds.summary: GALLERY, all seven contact sheets read three times over — once, then again after each round of replacements, because removing an object renumbers every cell after it and a verdict list keyed to cell numbers goes stale the moment it is applied. 175 files rejected, 76 (language, subject) pairs retired. 1,487 objects at the start of this audit, 844 now, across 269 languages.

rounds.title: The gallery audit, looked at: 135 objects rejected by eye across all seven sheets
rounds.summary: Every plate in the collection was laid out as numbered contact sheets and read. 135 files rejected, recorded in data/gallery/rejected.json with the language each was standing on, so a later fetch cannot quietly undo the audit.

rounds.title: An image audit: an empty case is better than a wrong exhibit
rounds.summary: August looked at the objects and found what a licence gate cannot see — portraits of people whose only connection to a language is a shared Commons category, irrelevant graphics, and the covers of academic works about a language rather than anything written in it. He was right, and the plate for Atlantic-Congo, the largest family in the atlas, was an MTN WiFi hotspot billboard. Araucanian's was a swimming pool. Bavarian's was a photograph of an egg with two words on it.

rounds.title: Objects 242 to 404 languages, letters 544 to 615 — by widening the probe, not by guessing
rounds.summary: Per-element coverage, measured: words 78.4%, letters 7.1%, prose 5.6%, audio 4.1%, objects 3.2%, timelines 0.8%. So objects and letters were the two real holes, and each had a different cause.

rounds.title: Every language now has something said about it: 36% to 100%
rounds.summary: THE MEASUREMENT. 8,618 language nodes, 7,970 carrying a description field — which reads as 92% coverage until you read them. 4,627 say the single word "language". 648 say nothing. 62 say "language in Papua". Filtering for anything over sixteen characters that is not a bare classification leaves 3,090: real coverage was 36%, and the same test on branches gave 19%.

rounds.title: Why fifty things are called Mixtec — a family card, and the answer computed rather than authored
rounds.summary: August opened Otomanguean, saw 181 languages of which 56 end in Zapotec and 53 in Mixtec — Juxtlahuaca Mixtec, Amoltepec Mixtec, Chazumba Mixtec, Silacayoapan Mixtec — and asked what that means. Nothing on screen explained it, and it is the single most confusing thing about this tree.

rounds.title: Objects open large, in the middle of this page
rounds.summary: August: clicking a picture should expand it in the centre of the screen, and should not go to an outside link. The wall images were wrapped in an anchor to Wikimedia Commons with target=_blank, which threw the visitor out of the museum to look at an exhibit already in front of them. The plate at the top of a card was not clickable at all.

rounds.title: Round 7 in the register: what shipped, what was found, what stays open
rounds.summary: Records the three new gates and their numbers, and the six bug classes this round produced — the ISO-macrolanguage/Glottolog mismatch that all three new tiers hit independently, the licence-gate-cannot-check-subject finding, sort order as a content decision, cache-raw-interpret- later, the truthy "[]", and the gallery manifest nothing had ever copied into web/data.

rounds.title: Audio: 15 languages to 313, and the word you hear is a word you can read
rounds.summary: August asked to add spoken audio to more languages and fix the ones that don't work. The 15 that shipped all worked — the five that failed a test here were my own script tripping Commons' rate limit, not broken links. The real defect was coverage: 15 languages out of 7,672.

rounds.title: 976 objects, 344 dated events, 316 encyclopedias — and the measurement that said where to look
rounds.summary: August asked for more pictures, artefacts and descriptions, especially for languages in current use, and for more factual content throughout. So the first thing built was a way to find out where the museum was thin, rather than guessing.

rounds.title: The letters of 544 languages, and a gate that checks they are the right letters
rounds.summary: August asked for alphabets everywhere possible. Two tiers, and the difference between them is the point. CURATED: Unicode CLDR exemplarCharacters, 291 languages — a claim about the language, agreed by people who write it. OBSERVED: the character inventory measured off the UDHR prose already shipped here, 253 more — a measurement of a document, labelled as one, with its sample size, and it never calls itself an alphabet.

rounds.title: A phrase tier for the languages ASJP cannot reach, starting with r n km.t
rounds.summary: August asked whether words could be added to r n km.t and found a real structural gap: ASJP samples living speech, so all fifteen ancient languages in the museum had no word tier at all — Egyptian, Middle English, Old French, Oscan, Umbrian, Sogdian, Bactrian, Khotanese, Classical Tibetan, Old Burmese, Imperial Aramaic, Punic, Old Japanese — and two living ones ASJP simply never sampled, Latvian and Venetian.

rounds.title: Record the completed enrichment loop
Enrichment pass 8, final: Uto-Aztecan and the Americas — 242 labels, 158 objects
rounds.summary: 28 languages across the Americas, plus Ambulas, which last pass dropped rather than retarget to a name I had not verified.

rounds.title: Enrichment pass 7: Trans-New-Guinea and the Papuan families — 214 labels, 139 objects
rounds.summary: 22 Papuan languages, from the region that holds more distinct languages per square kilometre than anywhere on Earth. Fore, where kuru was traced to mortuary feasting and established that a misfolded protein can carry a disease; Oksapmin, which counts up one arm, across the head and down the other, twenty-seven named body parts in a fixed order; Kalam, which has about a hundred verbs in total and builds everything else by stringing them together; Yimas, whose ten noun classes and triple agreement make its grammar a standard reference for what human languages can do; Iatmul clans owning tens of thousands of hereditary names and arguing over them for days; Huli's pandanus language, a taboo vocabulary used only in the forest so that spirits do not overhear; Dani, the 1960s test case for whether language shapes colour perception; Ekari counting in base sixty; Golin's whistled register carrying a specific message across a valley; the Asmat bisj poles, carved for the unavenged dead and left to rot back into the swamp.

rounds.title: Enrichment pass 6: Atlantic-Congo and Mande — 192 labels, 130 objects
rounds.summary: 25 languages. Swahili's utendi poetry, written in Arabic script on the Lamu coast from the seventeenth century; the Ifa corpus, 256 chapters of memorised verse attached to patterns cast on a divining board; the ninth-century Igbo-Ukwu bronzes, cast by lost-wax centuries before European contact; the clicks that entered Zulu and Xhosa from the Khoisan languages their speakers married into — sounds that came into Bantu from outside; Great Zimbabwe, built by Shona speakers and attributed by colonial authorities to almost anyone else; a Kikongo catechism printed in 1556; Nsibidi, ideographs older than any European contact, used by the Ekpe society for messages outsiders were not meant to read; Ngugi wa Thiong'o writing his next novel on prison toilet paper in Gikuyu after abandoning English in 1977.

rounds.title: Enrichment pass 5: Uralic — 167 labels, 119 objects
rounds.summary: 24 Uralic languages, which is most of the family's notable members. Estonian's three degrees of length and its Singing Revolution; Hungarian, stranded among Indo-European by a ninth-century migration, with the Funeral Sermon of 1195 the oldest continuous Uralic text; five Saami languages, including Inari Saami, rescued by a language nest begun in 1997 when almost no children spoke it; Karelian, whose runo-singers actually supplied the Kalevala that became Finland's national poem; Votic and Ingrian, each down to a few dozen speakers; Liv, whose last native speaker died in 2013 and which left its mark on Latvian grammar; Komi-Zyrian and the Abur alphabet devised for it in 1372; Mansi's bear ceremony with a vocabulary ordinary speech may not touch; Nganasan, the northernmost language on the Eurasian mainland.

rounds.title: Enrichment pass 4: Austronesian — 143 labels, 104 objects
rounds.summary: 24 Austronesian languages. Five Formosan languages first, because Taiwan is the homeland and the deepest splits in the whole family are among the languages that stayed: Amis, Atayal, Paiwan, Tsou and Bunun, whose speakers sing an eight-part rising polyphony with no clear parallel anywhere. Then Kawi on palm leaf carrying the Ramayana into Southeast Asia; Javanese, with more first-language speakers than any language without a state; baybayin, which the friars replaced because it left final consonants unwritten; the Batak pustaha written on folded tree bark; the Bugis La Galigo, longer than the Mahabharata and still not fully published; Malagasy, whose closest relatives are in Borneo four thousand miles away, which is how we know who settled Madagascar; Hawaiian, banned in schools from 1896 and brought back from fewer than fifty child speakers; the two Treaty of Waitangi texts that do not say the same thing; and rongorongo, carved upside-down on every other line, never deciphered, its readers dead in the slave raids of the 1860s.

rounds.title: Enrichment pass 3: Afro-Asiatic — 119 labels, 89 objects
rounds.summary: 23 Afro-Asiatic languages given wall labels and artefacts. Ugaritic, whose abecedary tablet shows the alphabet already in the order Hebrew, Greek and Latin still use; Phoenician, the traders who exported it; Imperial Aramaic, which is why a letter survives from a Jewish garrison on an island in the Nile; Classical Syriac, through which much of Aristotle reached Baghdad; Ge'ez and the Garima Gospels; Coptic and the Nag Hammadi jar; Maltese, the only Semitic language in Latin letters and the only one official in the EU; Tifinagh, kept alive largely by Tuareg women who taught it; Hausa in ajami and in Latin, both still in use; Somali, which had no official script until 1972 after decades of argument; Oromo, banned from writing in Ethiopia until 1991; Punic, still spoken in Augustine's North Africa six hundred years after Carthage fell; Hebrew, the only language with no native speakers ever to acquire millions again.

rounds.title: Enrichment pass 2: Sino-Tibetan — 96 labels, 73 objects
rounds.summary: 24 Sino-Tibetan languages given wall labels and artefacts. Cantonese keeping the finals that make Tang poetry rhyme; Hokkien's Peh-oe-ji, in which a literate population published newspapers for a century; Wu, with more speakers than Italian and official status nowhere; Classical Tibetan, whose spelling froze in the seventh century so the orthography is a fossil of the older language; the Myazedi inscription, the Rosetta Stone of mainland Southeast Asia; Tangut, a script of six thousand characters designed to look like Chinese and be unreadable to Chinese, recovered from the dead city of Khara-Khoto; Meitei Mayek, a script burned in the eighteenth century and put back into schools in the 2000s; the Fraser alphabet for Lisu, upright and upside-down Latin capitals and nothing else; Naxi Dongba, the only pictographic writing still in ritual use anywhere.

rounds.title: Enrichment pass 1: Indo-European depth — 72 labels, 60 objects
rounds.summary: 24 more Indo-European languages given wall labels and artefacts: Middle English and the Ellesmere Chaucer, Old Prussian (the Baltic language that died), Oscan and Umbrian, the Sogdian Ancient Letters abandoned in a watchtower near Dunhuang, Bactrian in Greek letters, Khotanese, Kashmiri's verb-second word order, Upper Sorbian's surviving dual, Cornish and Manx (both declared dead and both with children speaking them again), Faroese, West Frisian, Occitan's troubadours, Galician, Logudorese Sardinian's Latin hard c, Venetian, Slovenian's Freising manuscripts, Macedonian, Sindhi's implosives, Gujarati, Odia's rounded letters and the palm leaf that caused them, Assamese, Kurdish.

rounds.title: Navigability: languages open as languages, and the story becomes a storybook
rounds.summary: CLICKING A LANGUAGE OPENED A BRANCH CARD. The test for "is this a fork" was "does it have children" — but Glottolog gives most languages dialect children, so clicking Swedish gave you a branch of the family and you had to click again to reach the language. A fork is a node whose LEVEL is family; a language is a language, dialects or not. Swedish now opens as svenska with its 33 words on the first click.

rounds.title: Record round 12
A collapsible tree, and 48 languages with labels, objects and texts
rounds.summary: THE TREE IS TACTILE NOW. Indo-European opens showing its branches, not 586 tips at once: 18 rows, ten of them buds drawn as filled circles with their size on them. Click a bud and it opens - Germanic goes from one circle to 181 rows - and the same click puts that branch's card in the exhibit, with what it is, how many live and how many died under it, its earliest written member and a map of where its languages are recorded. Click again to close. One gesture, two useful results.

rounds.title: Record round 11: D9 closed, register empty
Seven museum labels were on the wrong language. Fixed, and gated.
rounds.summary: Verifying D9 on the live site surfaced this: nucl1301 is TURKISH, not Standard Arabic, so a paragraph about the Qur'an had been displayed on Turkish. Checking all thirty found seven wrong - the Maya codex image sat on Classical Syriac, the Kojiki on Sinitic, Old English on Early Irish, Hindi on Japanese, Classical Nahuatl on Classical Mandaic.

rounds.title: D9 closed: autonyms now reach 93% of speakers
rounds.summary: The register's last open item. Coverage was 11.2% of languages and the CLDR attempt last round returned zero locales.

rounds.title: Record round 10
Fix the shipped SyntaxError in tree.js, and gate JS parsing before publish
rounds.summary: I shipped a redeclared const. Re-adding the audio block to exhibit() introduced a second `au` alongside the existing autonym variable, tree.js threw on load, and the whole genealogy view came up empty on the live site. Every other gate checks DATA, so nothing noticed that the application itself did not parse.

rounds.title: C10 closed: the intervals were 3x too narrow. Story-view fix, D3 audio.
rounds.summary: C10 - SPATIAL DEPENDENCE. Moran's I on richness +0.360, and on the negative-binomial residuals +0.386: the model absorbs none of the spatial structure, so the worry admitted last round was not hypothetical. A spatial block bootstrap - 10-degree blocks resampled with replacement so neighbours stay together - gives the honest intervals:

rounds.title: Record round 9
C4 and C8 closed; fork cards; and a STORY view of Indo-European
rounds.summary: C4 - THE LITERATURE CHECK, verified against the source rather than recalled. Hua, Greenhill, Cardillo, Schneemann & Bromham, Nature Communications 10:2047 (2019), find that "climate has a much stronger effect on language diversity than landscape features, such as altitudinal range and river density", supporting the ecological risk hypothesis. That is our result: growing season +0.470 and peak NDVI +0.347 against ruggedness +0.155, roughly 3:1, same directions. WP-02 sets the two side by side.

rounds.title: Record round 8
Real orthography and IPA, D5 typology, artefact vignettes on the tree; D3 withheld
rounds.summary: ORTHOGRAPHY - the "typos" were mine. The word grids were showing ASJPcode: `3sat` for star, `t"3rs` for tooth, `k"3t"3l` for leaf. That is a coarse ASCII comparison scheme, not a spelling of anything, and displayed as a word it reads as a broken字. ASJP's CLDF already carries a `Segments` column with the same forms mapped to IPA, so all 380,912 forms across 6,110 languages are now shown in the International Phonetic Alphabet and labelled "as spoken - how the word sounds, not how it is spelled".

rounds.title: Record round 7
E1 and A7 closed; the gallery, museum labels, and a world locator
rounds.summary: E1 - THE INDEPENDENT WITNESS, planned for round 1 and built now. Our language positions are scored against a genuinely separate compilation, Wikidata's P625, for the 583 languages both catalogues carry: median displacement 22.7 km, 90th percentile 227 km, 77.2% agree within 100 km, 18 disagree by more than 500 km. The worst are linguistically explicable rather than random - Gothic 1,430 km, Cheyenne and Shawnee ~1,320 km (pre-removal homeland vs reservation), Sanskrit 915 km - which is what a useful witness looks like. Its two limits are printed with the result: Wikidata covers the better-known languages, and it is not fully independent. Selftest ratchets the median and the agreement rate, so our coordinates cannot move without the witness moving first.

rounds.title: Record round 6
A light atlas, richer exhibits, and each language's own map
rounds.summary: GROUND IS NOW LIGHT. The Earth renders as a paper atlas: pale ocean, parchment land, biome hues lifted 42% toward the page, the sun term halved with a large ambient so relief still reads without anything going to black. Family hues darkened to 0.62 so they sit as ink on paper rather than glowing. All chrome - rails, cards, About - is paper too.

rounds.title: Record round 5
Fix the genealogy layout below 900px: stacked panels painted over each other
rounds.summary: A grid ROW does not clip its child. When the three columns became three rows the panels had no min-height:0 and no scroll container of their own, so each one painted straight over the next — the exhibit landed on top of the tree head and the family list ran under the search box. Every stacked panel is now told it may be shorter than its content.

rounds.title: A museum of human language: the tree on paper, words for 6,110 languages
rounds.summary: THE TREE IS A TREE. The genealogy was an indented index. An index tells you a language has a parent; it does not show you that a family is mostly extinct. It is now drawn with organic tapering branches where THICKNESS is the number of living descendants and distance from the left is depth of descent, so the shape of a family reads before a single label does. Hollow tips are extinct languages, amber are endangered. Pan, zoom, click a leaf.

rounds.title: Record round 4 in the register and handoff
C9: negative binomial, and a correction to the round-3 statistics
rounds.summary: Poisson reported dispersion 8-20, which makes its standard errors about four times too narrow — the effect sizes were quotable and were quoted, the intervals were not. NB2 gives intervals that mean something and every term survives: growing season +1.67+-0.05 (z=33), absolute latitude -1.48+-0.04 (z=-41), ruggedness +0.48+-0.02 (z=20); all three plus greenness explain 49% of deviance.

rounds.title: The genealogy: a tree of every family, with time depth, scripts and texts
rounds.summary: THE TREE. The map answers where; this answers where from. A second view (WORKING-RULES §13b permits an abstract space only as a secondary one) over Glottolog's full classification: 429 top-level groups, 183 of them isolates, 8,618 languages and 13,706 dialects, 1,239 extinct and 2,573 endangered. Same glottocodes and the same family hues as the map, and clicking any language flies the map back to the ground it is spoken on. Built entirely from data already local — values.csv carries a Newick subtree per languoid.

rounds.title: Record round 3 in the register and handoff
16384x8192 tile pyramid, measured surface fields, autonyms, and the climate result
rounds.summary: RESOLUTION. The grid goes from 4096x2048 (9.8 km) to 16384x8192 (2.44 km) — 76% of ETOPO1's native resolution, 16x the pixels. One raster that size is 215 MB, so the fields ship as a four-level tile pyramid with a 1 px skirt: level 0 is 5.3 MB and paints the world at once, and only the tiles under the viewer's eye are fetched.

rounds.title: A5 attribution ledger, measured coverage, A4 enforced; correct the A1/A2 register rows
rounds.summary: The ledger is a module, not prose: build_site.py regenerates web/data/attribution.json from attribution.py and refuses to publish on any drift. Five ingested sources, every licence read at its source — which is what forced Ecoregions 2017's CC-BY-4.0 to be verified rather than assumed.

rounds.title: Record round 2 in the register, staged-changes, research README and handoff
Size the canvas with CSS viewport units, not from its own attribute
rounds.summary: A canvas is a replaced element, so position:fixed;inset:0 leaves width:auto resolving to the intrinsic attribute width. Setting the CSS size in vw/vh makes clientWidth independent of cv.width, so reading it to size the drawing buffer can no longer feed back.

rounds.title: Round 2 + build: the lit-terrain substrate and the language field
rounds.summary: The app is no longer the scaffold's dots on flat ground. It composes the surface per pixel in a fragment shader from four field rasters: 16-bit elevation (register B3's measured decision), biome, population, and family/diversity/documentation/coverage per snapshot.

rounds.title: Reposition fig-02 caption clear of the bar labels
Fix label collision in fig-02
Handoff: round 1 complete, C5 (the claim amendment) is blocking
Round 1: frames, licence gate, encoding measurement, diversity spine
